title: A clause you never signed
subtitle: Equal pay, the sex equality clause and the material factor defence
objectives: Explain how the s 66 sex equality clause operates and state the three routes to establishing a comparator's equal work
Distinguish 'like work', 'work rated as equivalent' and 'work of equal value' as three separate gateways into an equal pay claim
Apply the material factor defence, including its limits where the factor is itself tainted by sex discrimination, to a new fact pattern

leadingAuthorities.role: The statutory equal pay scheme: the sex equality clause, the three equal work gateways, and the material factor defence

leadingAuthorities.citation: Birmingham City Council v Abdulla [2012] UKSC 47
leadingAuthorities.role: Confirms equal pay claims may be brought in the ordinary courts, not only the employment tribunal, once the tribunal time limit has passed

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Equal pay looks like an application of ordinary sex discrimination law, but it runs on entirely separate statutory machinery — a term implied into every contract, not a claim about a discriminatory act. Where the profile shows knowledge is ahead of application, this brief note appears: 'You know the sex equality clause exists — this lesson tests whether you can actually run the three-gateway, then-defence structure on messy facts.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well on recall here before. The test pool below leans hard on scenarios: identifying which gateway applies, then testing whether a material factor defence actually holds up.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Start with Part 1 and be precise about what the sex equality clause actually does — it's a term implied into the contract, not a discrimination claim in the ordinary sense, and that distinction underpins everything else in this lesson.

overview.hook: Nobody negotiates the term at the centre of this lesson. It isn't in any offer letter, any contract, any staff handbook — and yet it sits in every single contract of employment in Great Britain, silently, whether the employer likes it or not. Equal pay law works by rewriting contracts from the outside, and understanding how it does that is the key to this whole area.
overview.lawStatedNotice: Law stated as at 24 September 2026. Sections 64-71 Equality Act 2010 are the stable, long-settled equal pay framework; no legislative change to the core scheme is currently pending.

parts.heading: A clause the statute writes for you
parts.voice: structural — establishes the mechanism before anything else
body: Equal pay claims don't work like the discrimination claims covered in the last three lessons. There's no PCP, no 'because of' test, no s 26 conduct requirement. Instead, s 66 Equality Act 2010 implies a sex equality clause into every contract of employment, whether the parties wrote one in or not, and whether they wanted one or not.

The mechanism is deceptively simple. If a term of A's contract is less favourable than a corresponding term in a comparator B's contract, where B is of the opposite sex and does 'equal work' to A, the sex equality clause automatically modifies A's term so that it is no less favourable. The claim isn't framed as 'my employer discriminated against me' in the way a s 13 claim is — it's framed as 'a term implied by statute into my own contract has been breached,' which is why equal pay claims can, in certain circumstances, be brought as an ordinary breach of contract claim in the civil courts as well as in the employment tribunal.

This term-by-term, contract-modifying structure explains a lot of the technical detail that follows in this lesson: why you need a real comparator (not a hypothetical one, unlike direct discrimination), why the claim is scoped to 'equal work' rather than any general fairness standard, and why the employer's only real escape route is a defence built into the same statutory scheme.

components.text: (1) If the terms of A's work do not (by whatever means) include a sex equality clause, they are to be treated as including one. (2) A sex equality clause is a provision that has the following effect — (a) if a term of A's is less favourable to A than a corresponding term of B's is to B, A's term is modified so as not to be less favourable...
elements: A sex equality clause is implied into every contract of employment, automatically
It compares A's terms with a real comparator B of the opposite sex doing equal work
Where A's term is less favourable than B's corresponding term, A's term is modified to match it
The claim is framed as a breach of an implied contractual term, not as an act of discrimination

components.definition: Unlike direct discrimination under s 13, an equal pay claim under the sex equality clause requires an actual comparator of the opposite sex doing equal work — a hypothetical comparator will not do.

interaction.prompt: Can an equal pay claim under s 66 be based on a hypothetical comparator, in the way a direct discrimination claim can?
options: No — a real comparator of the opposite sex doing equal work is required
Yes — a hypothetical comparator works equally well for equal pay claims
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. The sex equality clause modifies A's term by reference to B's actual corresponding term — there has to be a real B to compare against.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not quite — this is one of the sharpest differences from direct discrimination. Equal pay claims need an actual, identifiable comparator of the opposite sex doing equal work; a hypothetical one won't ground a s 66 claim.

parts.heading: Three doors into 'equal work'
parts.voice: structural — a reference-style part students will return to
body: Before the sex equality clause can do anything, the claimant must show they do 'equal work' to their chosen comparator. The Act recognises three, and only three, routes to establishing this, and they are genuinely different tests, not three ways of saying the same thing.

Like work means the work is the same or broadly similar, and any differences between what the claimant and comparator actually do are not of practical importance. Work rated as equivalent means a job evaluation study, conducted under an analytical scheme (assessing factors like effort, skill and decision-making), has rated the two jobs as equivalent. Work of equal value is the broadest and most open-ended route: even where the jobs are entirely different in content and have never been subject to a job evaluation study, a tribunal can find them equal in value by assessing the demands made on the worker under headings such as effort, skill and decision-making.

'Work of equal value' is the gateway that does the most work in modern equal pay litigation, because it's the only route that allows genuinely different jobs — a cook and a shipyard painter, say, or a speech and language therapist and a pharmacist — to be compared at all. It typically requires expert, and often lengthy, evidence before a tribunal, which is part of why equal pay litigation has a reputation for running for years in complex, large-scale claims.

components.label: The three equal work gateways
points: Like work — the same or broadly similar work, with no differences of practical importance
Work rated as equivalent — a job evaluation study under an analytical scheme has rated the jobs as equivalent

Work of equal value — a tribunal assesses the demands of two different jobs (effort, skill, decision-making) and finds them equal in value, even with no job evaluation study and no similarity in content
All three are independent gateways — a claimant only needs to succeed through one

interaction.prompt: Order these three equal work gateways from the narrowest (most similarity required) to the broadest (least similarity required).
items: Like work — same or broadly similar work
Work rated as equivalent — rated equal by a job evaluation study
Work of equal value — entirely different jobs assessed as equal in demands
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right — like work needs genuine similarity in content, work rated as equivalent relies on a formal scheme having already found parity, and work of equal value can bridge completely different jobs by assessing their underlying demands.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Think about how much similarity in actual job content each gateway requires — like work needs the most, work of equal value needs none at all, provided the underlying demands are shown to be equal.

parts.heading: Abdulla: where an equal pay claim can be brought
parts.voice: case-narrative — tells the story before naming the doctrine
body: Birmingham City Council v Abdulla concerns a large group of predominantly female council employees — cleaners, caterers, care workers — who discovered they had been paid less than male colleagues in comparable roles under a bonus scheme that heavily favoured traditionally male-dominated jobs. By the time many of them brought claims, the six-month time limit for bringing an equal pay claim in the employment tribunal had already expired.

Rather than accept their claims were time-barred, the claimants issued proceedings in the ordinary civil courts instead, relying on the ordinary six-year limitation period for breach of contract claims — since, as Part 1 established, the sex equality clause operates as an implied contractual term, a breach of it is, in principle, an ordinary breach of contract.

The council argued the county court should decline jurisdiction and strike the claims out, on the basis that Parliament intended equal pay disputes to be resolved by the specialist employment tribunal. The Supreme Court disagreed. It held the civil courts do have jurisdiction to hear equal pay claims framed as breach of contract, and that the mere fact the tribunal route was time-barred was not, on its own, a good reason to strike out a claim properly brought in the civil courts within the ordinary limitation period.

components.factsShort: Female council employees, time-barred from an employment tribunal claim, sued for equal pay as breach of contract in the civil courts instead.
components.ratioShort: Equal pay claims can be brought in the ordinary courts as breach of an implied contractual term, and a tribunal claim being time-barred is not, by itself, grounds to strike out a civil claim brought within the six-year limitation period.

expanded.facts: A large group of Birmingham City Council employees, mostly women in roles such as cleaning, catering and care work, discovered a bonus scheme had systematically paid comparable male-dominated roles more. Many had missed the tribunal's six-month time limit for bringing an equal pay claim (running from the end of employment or, for those still employed, throughout employment) and instead issued breach of contract proceedings in the county court, relying on the six-year limitation period generally applicable to contract claims.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Supreme Court confirmed that a sex equality clause operates as an implied term of the contract, meaning a breach of it can be pursued as an ordinary breach of contract in the civil courts, which have concurrent jurisdiction with the employment tribunal over equal pay disputes. The court held there was no proper basis to strike out the claims merely because they could, at an earlier point, have been brought in the tribunal instead.
expanded.significance: Abdulla is important less for reshaping the substantive equal pay test than for confirming the practical reach of the contractual mechanism established by s 66 (then the Equal Pay Act 1970, materially replicated in the 2010 Act): because the sex equality clause is a genuine implied contractual term, claimants who miss the tribunal window are not automatically without a remedy.

interaction.prompt: What did the Supreme Court in Abdulla actually decide?
options: That equal pay claims can never be brought outside the employment tribunal
That the civil courts have jurisdiction to hear equal pay claims as breach of contract, and a time-barred tribunal claim does not by itself justify striking out a properly brought civil claim
That the six-month tribunal time limit for equal pay claims was unlawful and should be extended
interaction.trapExplanation: It's tempting to read Abdulla as abolishing the tribunal time limit, but it did nothing of the sort — the tribunal's six-month limit stands. What the case confirmed is that the civil courts have their own, independent jurisdiction over equal pay as ordinary contract claims, with their own (longer) limitation period.

parts.heading: The material factor defence
parts.voice: direct — works from the statute to the practical trap
body: Even where a claimant establishes equal work with a comparator and a less favourable term, the employer has one statutory escape route: showing the difference is genuinely due to a material factor that does not involve treating the claimant less favourably because of sex.

Two requirements sit inside that single sentence, and both must be satisfied. First, the factor must be material — a genuine, significant reason for the pay difference, not a sham or an afterthought reason produced after the claim is brought. Common examples include a genuine difference in qualifications, length of service, market forces requiring a premium to recruit for a scarce skill, or geographic location. Second — and this is where most application questions are actually won or lost — the factor must not itself involve, directly or indirectly, treating the claimant less favourably because of sex.

This second limb is what makes the defence genuinely narrow. An employer cannot rely on a factor that is itself tainted by sex discrimination, even unintentionally. If a pay differential is explained by, say, historic pay protection given to employees transferred from a legacy, predominantly male, pay scale, and that legacy scale itself reflected historic sex discrimination, the factor doesn't escape scrutiny just because it looks neutral on its face today — it must be objectively justified in the same way a PCP under s 19 must be, as a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim, where the factor is shown to have a disproportionate impact by sex.

components.text: The sex equality clause in A's terms has no effect in relation to a difference between A's terms and B's terms if the responsible person shows that the difference is because of a material factor which — (a) does not involve treating A less favourably because of A's sex than the responsible person treats B, and (b) if the factor is not shown to be a material difference to the case, in the case of an indirectly discriminatory factor, is a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim.
elements: The employer bears the burden of proving the material factor defence
The factor must be a genuine and significant explanation for the difference, not a sham
The factor must not itself involve treating A less favourably because of sex
Where the factor has a disproportionate impact by sex, it must be objectively justified as proportionate means of a legitimate aim

components.commonWrongAnswer: Students often conclude the material factor defence succeeds simply because the employer has identified a genuine, non-fabricated reason for the pay gap — such as 'she was recruited on a legacy pay scale' or 'his qualifications were different.'
components.whyItsWrong: A genuine, non-sham reason satisfies only the first limb of the defence. The factor must also not itself be tainted by sex discrimination — and if it is shown to have a disproportionate impact on one sex, the employer has to go further and objectively justify it, exactly as with an indirect discrimination defence. A 'genuine' explanation that turns out to perpetuate historic sex-based pay structures does not automatically clear this second hurdle.

interaction.prompt: An employer pays a male comparator more, explaining this is because he was recruited from a competitor at a higher salary during a skills shortage, with evidence of genuine market pressure at the time. How confident are you this material factor defence is likely to succeed?
interaction.explanation: Genuine market forces requiring a premium to recruit a scarce skill is a well-recognised material factor, and nothing in this fact pattern suggests the factor is itself tainted by sex discrimination — this is a comparatively strong defence, subject to the employer being able to evidence the market pressure was real.

parts.heading: Running the whole structure on one scenario
parts.voice: Socratic — walks through the full analysis, testing each stage
body: Put the whole structure together on one set of facts. Meera is a speech and language therapist employed by an NHS trust. She discovers that a male pharmacist employed by the same trust, on the same pay band structure, is paid more, despite her role never having been the subject of a formal job evaluation study and the two roles having almost nothing in common day to day.

Start with equal work. 'Like work' is a non-starter — the jobs aren't the same or broadly similar. 'Work rated as equivalent' is also unavailable, since there's no job evaluation study. That leaves 'work of equal value' as the only realistic gateway: Meera would need expert evidence comparing the demands of the two roles — effort, skill, responsibility, decision-making — to show they are, despite completely different content, equal in overall value. This is exactly the kind of genuinely different-job comparison the equal value gateway exists for.

Suppose the tribunal, on expert evidence, finds the two roles are indeed of equal value. The trust then raises a material factor defence, explaining the pharmacist is paid on a separate, historically higher-paid clinical pay spine inherited from a legacy pre-merger trust, itself never reviewed for equal pay compliance. That's a genuine, non-sham factor at the first limb — but the second limb is where the real fight happens: if that legacy pay spine can be shown to have developed along historically gendered lines (pharmacy having been a more male-dominated profession when the spine was set), the trust would need to objectively justify continuing to rely on it, not simply point to its historical origin as an automatic answer.

components.title: Running an equal pay claim end to end
components.description: The full analytical sequence from equal work to the material factor defence.

nodes.label: Identify a real comparator of the opposite sex on a more favourable term
Which equal work gateway applies? Like work / work rated as equivalent / work of equal value
None apply → no equal pay claim under s 66
Gateway established → sex equality clause modifies A's term, unless the employer proves a defence
Is there a genuine, non-sham material factor explaining the difference?
Yes → does the factor itself involve less favourable treatment because of sex, or have a disproportionate impact by sex?
Yes → must be objectively justified as proportionate means of a legitimate aim, or the defence fails

components.textAlternative: Start by identifying a real comparator of the opposite sex on a more favourable term. Then ask which equal work gateway applies: like work, work rated as equivalent, or work of equal value. If none fit, there is no claim. If one fits, the sex equality clause modifies the claimant's term unless the employer proves a material factor defence. First ask whether there is a genuine, non-sham factor explaining the difference — if not, the claim succeeds. If there is, ask whether that factor itself involves less favourable treatment because of sex, or has a disproportionate impact by sex. If it does, the employer must objectively justify it as a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim, or the defence fails. If the factor is clean of any sex taint, the defence succeeds and the claim fails.

interaction.prompt: In Meera's scenario, if the legacy pay spine is found to have developed along historically gendered lines, what must the trust show to succeed on the material factor defence?
options: That continuing to apply the pay spine is a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim
Nothing further — a genuine historical explanation is automatically sufficient
That the pay spine was set by an external body rather than the trust itself
interaction.explanation: Once a material factor is shown to have a disproportionate impact by sex, the employer must clear the same objective justification hurdle used in indirect discrimination — a genuine historical origin, by itself, does not satisfy this second limb of the defence.

testPool.prompt: Name the statutory provision that implies a sex equality clause into every contract of employment, and state what it does in one sentence.
acceptableAnswers: s 66 Equality Act 2010 — implies a term modifying less favourable terms to match a comparator of the opposite sex doing equal work
section 66, implies a sex equality clause modifying A's less favourable term to match B's
testPool.modelAnswer: Section 66 Equality Act 2010 implies a sex equality clause into every contract of employment, which modifies any term of A's contract that is less favourable than a corresponding term of a real comparator B of the opposite sex doing equal work.

testPool.prompt: Is an equal pay claim under s 66 framed as an act of discrimination or as a breach of an implied contractual term?
options: A breach of an implied contractual term
An act of discrimination in the same sense as direct discrimination

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the three statutory routes to establishing 'equal work'?
options: Like work
Work rated as equivalent
Work of comparable seniority
Work of equal value
testPool.trapExplanation: 'Work of comparable seniority' isn't a recognised gateway at all — the three statutory routes are like work, work rated as equivalent, and work of equal value. Seniority might be relevant evidence within one of those tests, but it isn't a gateway in its own right.

testPool.prompt: Under s 69, what two things must an employer show to succeed on the material factor defence?
options: A genuine material factor explaining the difference, which does not itself involve less favourable treatment because of sex (or, if it has a disproportionate impact by sex, is objectively justified)
Only that the pay difference was not intentional
Only that the comparator was recruited more recently

testPool.prompt: Order the analytical steps in a full equal pay claim.
items: Identify a real comparator of the opposite sex on a more favourable term
Establish equal work through one of the three statutory gateways
The sex equality clause modifies the claimant's term unless the employer proves a defence
Assess whether the employer's material factor defence succeeds, including objective justification if the factor is sex-tainted

testPool.prompt: In the passage below, drawn from the reasoning in Abdulla, highlight the sentence stating the ratio on jurisdiction.
testPool.passage: The claimants' equal pay claims were time-barred in the employment tribunal, so they issued proceedings in the county court instead. A sex equality clause operates as an implied term of the contract, meaning a breach of it can be pursued as an ordinary breach of contract in the civil courts, which have concurrent jurisdiction with the employment tribunal over equal pay disputes.
testPool.ratioSentence: A sex equality clause operates as an implied term of the contract, meaning a breach of it can be pursued as an ordinary breach of contract in the civil courts, which have concurrent jurisdiction with the employment tribunal over equal pay disputes.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that shows this claim must rely on the 'work of equal value' gateway rather than 'like work' or 'work rated as equivalent.'
testPool.scenarioText: Farah, a hospital radiographer, and Oliver, a hospital estates engineer, have entirely different day-to-day roles, and no job evaluation study has ever compared the two positions. Farah believes, based on the effort, skill and responsibility each role demands, that the jobs are of equal value.
tappableSpans: no job evaluation study has ever compared
effort, skill and responsibility each role demands
that the jobs are of equal value
testPool.correctSpan: no job evaluation study has ever compared
testPool.feedbackCorrect: Right — the absence of a job evaluation study rules out 'work rated as equivalent,' and the entirely different day-to-day content rules out 'like work,' leaving 'work of equal value' as the only available gateway, assessed by demands rather than content.
testPool.feedbackIncorrect: Focus on what rules out the other two gateways specifically. The absence of any job evaluation study is what forecloses 'work rated as equivalent,' leaving 'work of equal value' as the remaining route.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario more clearly establishes 'like work' rather than requiring the 'work of equal value' gateway?
testPool.scenarioA: Two receptionists at the same firm perform identical front-desk duties on the same shift pattern, save for minor differences in which phone lines they answer.
testPool.scenarioB: A structural engineer and a HR business partner at the same firm have never had their roles compared by any job evaluation scheme and perform entirely different day-to-day tasks.
testPool.explanation: A is a straightforward like work case: the roles are broadly similar with no differences of practical importance. B involves genuinely different jobs with no job evaluation study, which can only be compared, if at all, through the work of equal value gateway.

testPool.prompt: An employer pays a male warehouse supervisor more than a female colleague doing identical work, explaining only that 'he asked for more money and we agreed.' Is this likely to succeed as a material factor defence?
options: It is weak — 'he asked for more' alone, without more, risks being treated as a proxy for unequal bargaining that courts have been wary of accepting uncritically as a standalone material factor
It automatically succeeds, because any genuine negotiation outcome is a material factor
It automatically fails, because negotiated pay can never be a material factor
testPool.explanation: A bare 'they negotiated harder' explanation, without more context (such as evidencing a genuine, sex-neutral reason the negotiation succeeded), is a recognised weak spot in material factor defences — tribunals scrutinise whether such reasons mask factors that track sex rather than genuinely explaining the difference.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that makes this qualification difference likely to succeed as a material factor defence.
testPool.explanation: The defence turns on the factor being both genuinely explanatory of the pay difference and untainted by sex — a role-relevant qualification gap only succeeds as a material factor once it is shown to be unconnected to sex; relevance alone is not enough.
testPool.scenarioText: An employer explains a pay difference by pointing to a genuine difference in professional qualifications between the claimant and her comparator. The qualification is directly relevant to the demands of the role, is held by the comparator but not the claimant, and there is clear evidence it is unconnected to either employee's sex.
tappableSpans: directly relevant to the demands of the role
clear evidence it is unconnected to either employee's sex
testPool.correctSpan: clear evidence it is unconnected to either employee's sex

testPool.prompt: Once a material factor is shown to have a disproportionate impact by sex, must the employer additionally show it is a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim?
options: Yes — the factor must then be objectively justified in the same way as an indirectly discriminatory PCP
No — showing the factor is genuine is always enough, regardless of its impact

testPool.prompt: Sadia, a clinical coding officer at an NHS trust, learns that a male IT systems analyst in the same pay band is paid more. No job evaluation study has compared the two roles, but Sadia believes, based on the analytical demands, decision-making and responsibility involved in each, that the roles are equal in value. The trust's stated explanation is that IT roles are paid on a separate, market-driven pay scale set decades ago when IT was almost entirely staffed by men, and the scale has never been reviewed since. Analyse Sadia's prospects of success in an equal pay claim.
factsToOrder: Sadia and the comparator are in genuinely different roles with no job evaluation study
Sadia believes the roles are equal in value based on their underlying demands
The IT pay scale was set decades ago when the profession was overwhelmingly male
The scale has never been reviewed since it was set
The trust relies on the separate pay scale as its explanation for the difference

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
Issue given only; student selects the Rule, drags facts into Application, writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether Sadia can establish equal work with her comparator through the work of equal value gateway, and whether the trust's material factor defence, based on a historic pay scale, is likely to succeed.
modelAnswer.rule: Equal work can be established via like work, work rated as equivalent, or work of equal value (ss 64-65); the sex equality clause under s 66 then modifies the less favourable term unless the employer shows a genuine material factor under s 69 that does not itself involve less favourable treatment because of sex, or, if it has a disproportionate impact by sex, is objectively justified as a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim.
modelAnswer.application: With no job evaluation study and genuinely different job content, work of equal value is the relevant gateway, and Sadia would need expert evidence on the comparative demands of the two roles. If equal value is established, the trust's reliance on a separate pay scale is a genuine, non-sham explanation on its face, satisfying the first limb of s 69. But the scale's origin in a historically male-dominated profession, never reviewed since, raises a real risk that it has a disproportionate impact by sex even today — which would require the trust to objectively justify continuing to apply it, rather than simply pointing to its historical existence.
modelAnswer.conclusion: Sadia has a viable claim via the work of equal value gateway, and the trust's material factor defence is vulnerable: a historic, unreviewed, gender-skewed pay scale is unlikely to be accepted as untainted without independent evidence of a current, legitimate, proportionate justification for maintaining it.

testPool.prompt: How confident are you that, once a material factor has a disproportionate impact by sex, it must meet the same objective justification standard used in indirect discrimination?
sliderLabels: Not confident — the two tests are unrelated
testPool.explanation: Correct. The second limb of s 69 deliberately imports the same proportionate-means-to-a-legitimate-aim standard used in indirect discrimination once a material factor is shown to have a disproportionate impact by sex — the two areas of law converge at exactly this point.

testPool.prompt: Name the leading case confirming equal pay claims can be brought in the ordinary courts as breach of contract, and state what it decided in one sentence.
acceptableAnswers: Birmingham City Council v Abdulla — confirmed the civil courts have jurisdiction over equal pay claims as breach of contract
Abdulla, holding the civil courts have concurrent jurisdiction with the employment tribunal over equal pay
testPool.modelAnswer: Birmingham City Council v Abdulla [2012] UKSC 47, which held that the civil courts have jurisdiction to hear equal pay claims as breach of an implied contractual term, and that a time-barred tribunal claim does not by itself justify striking out a properly brought civil claim.

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is treating a 'genuine' material factor as automatically sufficient to defeat an equal pay claim. A material factor defence has two limbs, not one — the factor must be genuine, and it must not itself be tainted by sex discrimination, with objective justification required wherever it has a disproportionate impact by sex.
